title: Walk the house before you hire anyone
summary: A slow walk with a notepad shows what to fix, what to tell buyers, and what to leave alone.
body: Start at the street. Look at the roof edge, the walkway, and the front door. Write down what you see before you explain it away.
Inside, run every faucet, flip every light, and open every window that should open. Note stains, soft floors, and doors that stick. One line per issue.

Sort the list into three piles: safety and function, things that will show up in photos, and projects you will not do. Ask for written bids on the jobs you cannot price yourself. A bid is a number you can type into the proceeds calculator. A hunch is not.
steps: Walk once with the lights on and once in daylight.
Write one line per issue.
Mark each line: fix, disclose, or leave.

title: Fix function before you spend on finish
summary: Repair leaks, heat, and latches before you buy paint.
body: Leaks, heat, cooling, loose steps, and dead outlets come before paint. A fresh coat on a damp wall does not hold, and buyers notice a door that will not latch.
If a system is near the end of its life, get it in writing and decide whether you will repair it or describe it in your disclosure. Do not hide it behind a rug.
Small function fixes are the ones people test on a first visit: a drain that clears, a garage door that reverses, a handrail that does not wobble.
steps: Stop active leaks first.
Test smoke and carbon-monoxide alarms.
Plan paint and floors only after the function list is done.

title: Clear surfaces before you add anything
summary: Empty counters and floors do more for a showing than extra decor.
body: Buyers are trying to see the room. Pack until each room has one job: sleeping, cooking, eating, or sitting.
Leave a few useful pieces. A made bed, a table that fits, and a lamp that works are enough. Take extra chairs out if the path is tight.
Store packed boxes outside the photo frame. A dining room full of bins reads as a storage room.
steps: Clear counters down to one or two useful items.
Pull furniture off the main walking path.
Keep packed boxes out of the rooms you will photograph.

title: Pack personal items before the first showing
summary: Box photos, mail, and papers so the rooms show the house.
body: Personal photos, mail, and collections pull attention away from the property. Box them before the first photographer or visitor arrives.
Take names, notes, and calendars off the refrigerator. Close closets you do not want opened, and do not overstuff the ones you leave.
Leave a simple path from the front door through the main rooms. If you still live there, pick one cupboard for daily items and keep the rest clear on showing days.
steps: Box personal papers and photos.
Clear the refrigerator door.
Walk from the front door to the back of the house and move anything that blocks the path.

title: Price the property you have
summary: Compare sold homes that match this property, then write the net you will accept.
body: Pull recent sold listings that match this house on facts you can check: bedroom count, bathrooms, size, lot, garage, age, and the updates the listing described.
Active listings are asking prices. Sold listings are closed prices. Use the closed ones as your comparison set, then adjust for condition you can see in the photos and at the property.

Write three numbers before you pick a list price: the price you will advertise, the net you hope to clear, and the lowest net you will accept. The lowest net belongs in the proceeds calculator, using your payoff and your costs.
steps: Compare at least three sold properties with similar facts.
Adjust for condition you can point to, not for a story.
Write the bottom net before the first offer.

title: Leave room to answer a real offer
summary: Set the list price with room for a credit and still hit your net.
body: A list price is the number on the ad. Your net is the decision. Price, credits, and timing move together.
If you set the list price at the exact dollar you need to walk away with, the first repair credit puts you under your line.
Decide in advance which givebacks you can live with: a repair credit, a closing-cost credit, or a later closing date. Write them down while you are calm.
steps: Keep the list price and the net you need on two separate lines.
Pick two terms you can flex on and one you will not.
Recalculate proceeds every time a credit changes.

title: Take listing photos in daylight with the lights on
summary: Open the shades, turn on the lamps, and keep the camera level.
body: The camera needs light. Open the window coverings and turn on the overhead lights and the lamps you are leaving.
Shoot when you can see the corners of the room. Glare on bare glass can wash a wall out. Wait for the sun to move off that window, or shoot that room from a different corner.
Stand in a corner and keep the camera level. If the walls lean in the frame, the room looks smaller than it is. Close toilet lids, move trash cans, and coil the hose if it sits in the front photo.
steps: Clean the windows you will shoot through.
Turn on the lights before you frame the shot.
Take one wide photo and one detail photo in each main room.

title: Photograph the work you finished
summary: Give finished repairs their own clear photo, and lead with the front of the house.
body: People scroll quickly. A clear photo of a repaired step, a new faucet, or the label on a replaced water heater answers a question before the showing.
Do not feature a project you have not finished. An open wall belongs in the disclosure conversation, not as the first image.
Lead the set with the best daylight photo of the front. Then show the kitchen, each bathroom, and the main living space before the extra rooms.
steps: Put the front of the house first.
Include one clear photo of each bathroom and the kitchen.
Retake any shot where the repair is blurry or dark.

title: List the jobs before you pick who does them
summary: Write every job in a sale, then decide who will do it and what it costs you.
body: Hiring an agent and selling it yourself are two ways to cover the same work: pricing, photos, showings, disclosure forms, offer review, negotiation, and closing coordination.

Next to each job, write the name of the person who will do it and what it will cost you in hours or dollars. Use your own rates in the commission comparison. This site does not fill in a rate for you.
If you sell it yourself, you can still offer to pay a buyer’s agent. That choice is a line you enter. It is not a requirement and it is not a default.
steps: Make two columns: the job, and who owns it.
Ask any agent you interview for a written list of what they will do.
Decide who owns each job before you order a sign.

title: Questions to answer if you sell it yourself
summary: Forms, showings, and offer review are still yours if you sell without an agent.
body: Find out which disclosure forms your state expects. A local attorney or the closing company can tell you which forms apply. This site cannot.
Decide how a buyer books a showing, where you will be during the visit, and what you will put away first. Set hours you can actually keep.
Plan the offer path before the first one arrives: who receives the contract, who reads it with you, and how quickly you will answer.
steps: Ask a closing company what they need from a seller who has no agent.
Write your showing hours down.
Have an attorney or agent review the first contract before you sign it.

title: Read the whole offer before you answer the price
summary: Credits, dates, and contingencies change the money more than the headline price.
body: Find the purchase price, seller credits, earnest money, financing terms, and every date. Read those before you react to the price alone.
A higher price with a large credit can leave you with less than a lower price with no credit. Run both sets of numbers through the proceeds calculator before you reply.
A repair request is a request. It is not a promise you already made. List what you will do, what you will credit, and what you will decline.
steps: Highlight every dollar that leaves your side.
Highlight every deadline.
Ask your agent or attorney what each contingency lets the buyer do.

title: Compare net and dates before you counter
summary: Put each offer on one row and counter the gap in your net.
body: Make one row per offer: price, credits, closing date, and what has to happen first, such as an inspection, an appraisal, or a loan approval.
Choose the row that meets the net you wrote down and a timeline you can move on. If none do, counter the specific gap in plain numbers.
Answer before the offer expires. If you need more time, ask for it in writing. Do not let a deadline pass in silence if you still want that offer.
steps: Build one comparison row per offer.
Recalculate proceeds after every counter.
Send your answer in writing.

title: Build the closing folder before you have a buyer
summary: Collect payoff contacts, receipts, and a wire-check plan before you are under contract.
body: Start a folder, paper or digital, for the mortgage servicer’s payoff phone number, the association contact if you have one, warranty paperwork you plan to transfer, and receipts for repairs you are disclosing.
Keep your disclosure draft in that folder and update it when a repair is finished. The version you sign should match the house on signing day.
Ask the closing company how they send wire instructions. Plan to confirm those instructions by calling a phone number you look up yourself, not a number that arrived only in an email.
steps: Give the folder one home and label each document.
Request the payoff when you have a contract and a closing date.
Call the closing office to confirm wiring instructions before you send money.

title: Walk the house again before the buyer’s final visit
summary: Check the fixtures you promised to leave, and report anything that broke.
body: Test the lights, the appliances you are leaving, and the faucets. Replace bulbs that are out. The final walkthrough is easier when you have already done this.
Remove trash, leftover paint, and hardware you are not including. The contract says what stays. Do not remove a fixture you agreed to leave.
If something broke after you signed, tell the buyer in writing before they find it. A surprise at the walkthrough is harder to solve than a note sent the day before.
steps: Use the same room list you used for showings.
Leave remotes, keys, and codes where the contract says they go.
Do a last pass for personal papers in drawers.

title: Book the move after the closing date is real
summary: Wait for a contract date, then book the truck with a written backup plan.
body: A target date can move. Put a deposit on a mover when the closing date is in the contract, and ask what happens if that date shifts by a day or two. Get the answer in writing.
Measure sofas, mattresses, and tables that might not fit through the next door. Do this before the truck is in the driveway.

If you are packing yourself, start with rooms you do not use every day. Keep a first-night box in your car: chargers, a change of clothes, basic tools, and anything you need before the truck is unpacked.
steps: Confirm the closing date with the closing company before you book.
Get the mover’s cancellation terms in writing.
Pack the first-night box and keep it with you.

title: Label boxes by the room they go to
summary: Name the room on two sides of every box and keep a first-night box with you.
body: Write the room and a short contents line. “Kitchen — pans” is enough. Write it on two sides so a stack does not hide the label.
Number the boxes and keep a simple list on your phone or on paper. When a box is missing, the number tells you what to ask about.
Carry documents, jewelry, and spare keys in the car. Do not put them on the truck.
steps: Label at least two sides of each box.
Number the boxes and keep the list.
Load the first-night box last so it comes off first.

title: Replace cracked caulk before photo day
summary: Cracked caulk shows up in close photos. Replace it while the repair list is still short.
body: Look along tubs, showers, and the kitchen sink. Cracked or missing caulk reads as a leak even when the wall behind it is dry.
Remove the old bead, let the joint dry, and lay a new one. A thin, smooth line photographs better than a thick smear.
If you find soft drywall while you are there, stop and treat that as a leak repair, not a caulk job. Put it on the function list.
steps: Check every wet joint with the lights on.
Recaulk only after the joint is dry.
Photograph the finished joint for your repair folder.

title: Finish the entry before the rest of the house
summary: The front door and entry are the first rooms a visitor stands in. Finish those before the back closets.
body: Wash the door, polish or replace tired hardware, and make sure the house numbers can be read from the street. A stuck storm door is a first impression you can fix in an afternoon.
Clear shoes, mail, and coats down to what you use this week. One mat and a working light are enough.
If you only have one day before photos, spend it on the entry, the kitchen counters, and the main bathroom. Leave the deep closet for later.
steps: Clean the door and the hardware.
Check that the entry light works.
Remove the daily clutter before every showing, not only before the photo shoot.

title: Write your bottom line before the first showing
summary: Write the lowest net you will accept, and do it before anyone asks.
body: Open the proceeds calculator and type your payoff, the commissions you expect to pay, closing costs, credits, and repairs. The result is a draft of your net, not a promise.
Write the lowest net you will accept on paper and put it with your offer checklist. Change it only when a real number in the deal changes.
When an offer arrives, you already know which gaps matter. You will not have to invent a bottom line while someone waits on the phone.
steps: Enter your own costs in the calculator.
Write the lowest acceptable net where you can find it.
Update it when the payoff or a credit changes, not when you feel rushed.

title: Keep the camera level and skip the distortion
summary: A tilted wide shot makes a straight room look small. Keep the camera level.
body: Hold the phone or camera at about chest height and level with the floor. If you tilt up, the ceiling takes over the photo. If you tilt down, the floor does.
Step back before you zoom with your feet. Extreme wide angles bow straight lines. A buyer who visits will notice that the room does not match the picture.
Take two frames of each room and keep the one where the door casing is vertical. Delete the other so it does not end up in the listing by mistake.
steps: Use a level line in the room, such as a door frame, to check the camera.
Shoot from a corner, not from the middle of the room.
Keep the frame that matches what a person sees when they walk in.

title: Put every deadline on one page
summary: Every offer has dates. Put them on one page so none expire in silence.
body: Copy each date out of the contract onto one page: offer expiration, earnest-money due date, inspection end, appraisal, loan commitment, and closing.
Add the name of the person who has to act. A date with no owner is easy to miss.
Check the page every morning while you are under contract. If a date is close and you are not ready, call your agent, attorney, or the closing company that day.
steps: Transfer dates the hour you receive an offer or a counter.
Name an owner for each date.
Look at the page before you agree to a new credit or a new closing day.

title: Call the closing office before you wire
summary: Look up the closing office and call them before you send a wire.
body: Wire instructions that arrive by email can be altered. Treat a last-minute change of bank details as a stop sign.

Look up the closing company’s phone number on its own site or on the paperwork you received at the start, then call. Read the routing number and account number back. Do not use a phone number that was only in the email.
If anything does not match, do not send the wire. Ask the closing officer to reissue the instructions in the way they normally do.
steps: Save the closing company’s main phone number when you open the file.
Call that number and read the wire details back.
Refuse rushed changes that you cannot confirm on the phone.

title: Deep-clean after the dusty work, not before
summary: Clean after the dusty repairs, not before. Archived because the prep tips now cover the order of work.
body: Sanding, patching, and caulk throw dust. If you deep-clean first, you will clean again after the last repair.
Do the messy jobs, let the dust settle, then clean top to bottom: lights and trim, then counters, then floors. Save the floor for last so you are not tracking grit back across it.
This note stays in the archive so the order is still written down. The active prep tips now carry the same sequence: function first, finish next, clean before photos.
steps: Finish dusty repairs before the deep clean.
Clean from the top of the room toward the floor.
Schedule photos after the floors are dry.
